title: 03 — Object Storage and Immutable Landing
html:
03 — Object Storage and Immutable Landing

The one idea: keep an untouchable copy of every file exactly as it arrived, named by the hash of its bytes, in storage that physically refuses to delete or overwrite it. Everything downstream can then be rebuilt, audited or disputed against that copy.

1. Object storage in five minutes

Object storage (Amazon S3, Azure Blob/ADLS Gen2, Google Cloud Storage, and S3-compatible servers such as MinIO, Ceph RGW, SeaweedFS or Garage) stores objects: a blob of bytes, a key, and metadata, inside a bucket.

Property Consequence for data engineering
No real directories — a/b/c.parquet is just a key with slashes "Listing a folder" is a prefix scan; renames are copy + delete, not atomic
Objects are immutable — you replace, never edit in place Table formats write new files and never modify old ones
Strong read-after-write consistency (S3 since 2020, Azure, GCS) A file you just wrote is immediately visible
Cheap, durable, effectively unlimited Storage is separated from compute: any engine can read it
High latency per request (tens of ms) Many small files are slow; prefer 128 MB–1 GB files

Because a rename is not atomic, object storage alone cannot give you a transactional table. That is the gap Apache Iceberg fills (chapter 05).

2. Immutable landing: definition and purpose

The landing zone (sometimes called raw or staging) is the first place an acquired file is stored. An immutable landing zone adds three rules:

  1. Store the original bytes — no parsing, no re-encoding, no "fixing" line endings.
  2. Name it by content — the object key contains the SHA-256 hash of the bytes.
  3. Lock it — the storage itself prevents deletion or overwrite for a retention period (WORM: Write Once, Read Many).

Why bother:

  • Reproducibility. Any table can be rebuilt from landing if a parser had a bug.
  • Evidence. When a number is disputed, you can show the exact file, byte-for-byte, and prove it has not changed since you received it.
  • Idempotency. The same file delivered twice has the same hash, so it is stored once and processed once.
  • Regulatory retention. Many financial record-keeping rules require tamper-proof retention for years.

3. Content addressing with SHA-256

import hashlib
from pathlib import Path

def sha256_of(path: Path, chunk: int = 1 << 20) -> str:
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with path.open("rb") as f:
        while block := f.read(chunk):
            h.update(block)
    return h.hexdigest()            # 64 hex characters

A key layout that works well:

s3://landing/
  source=amfi-nav/
    received=2026-10-31/
      sha256=9f2c…e41a/
        original.txt            ← the bytes, untouched
        manifest.json           ← who, where, when, licence, original filename
  • The hash is the identity of the file. Original filenames are metadata (NAVAll.txt arrives every day with different content).
  • Two levels of idempotency: file level (hash already seen → skip) and record level (natural key + content hash already loaded → skip).

3.1 The acquisition manifest

Every landed file gets a small JSON record, also written to a database table so it can be queried:

{
  "manifest_id": "01JBX7…",
  "sha256": "9f2c…e41a",
  "size_bytes": 1843301,
  "source_id": "amfi-nav",
  "source_url": "https://…/NAVAll.txt",
  "original_filename": "NAVAll.txt",
  "content_type": "text/plain",
  "received_at": "2026-10-31T18:05:12Z",
  "collector_version": "1.4.2",
  "licence_id": "public-terms-2026",
  "retention_until": "2033-10-31"
}

The manifest is the first link in lineage: every later row can carry manifest_id (or the hash) back to the file it came from.

4. A source and rights register

Before collecting, record what you are allowed to do with each source:

Column Example
source_id amfi-nav
owner Publisher name
access_method HTTPS download, API, SFTP, email, database CDC
licence_terms Store? Derive? Redistribute? Attribution?
licence_expires Date or none
schedule Daily 21:00 IST
contains_personal_data yes / no

The collector checks the register first and refuses to run if rights are missing or expired. This keeps legal decisions out of code and makes them auditable.

5. WORM: Object Lock

5.1 How S3 Object Lock works

  • Enabled when the bucket is created (it also forces versioning on).
  • Each object version can carry a retention (until a date) and/or a legal hold (until removed).
  • Two retention modes:
Mode Who can shorten or remove it Use for
Governance Users with a special bypass permission Testing, internal policies
Compliance Nobody, including the root account, until the date passes Regulatory records

An "overwrite" simply creates a new version — the locked version stays. A "delete" adds a delete marker — the locked version stays.

Azure equivalent: immutability policies on Blob containers (time-based retention, legal hold, version-level WORM).

5.2 Hands-on with MinIO

# compose.yaml
services:
  minio:
    image: minio/minio          # pin a version you have tested; check the project's current distribution terms
    command: server /data --console-address ":9001"
    environment:
      MINIO_ROOT_USER: admin
      MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD: password123
    ports: ["9000:9000", "9001:9001"]
    volumes: ["minio-data:/data"]
volumes:
  minio-data:

docker compose up -d
mc alias set local http://localhost:9000 admin password123

mc mb --with-lock local/landing                      # Object Lock + versioning, must be set at creation
mc retention set --default COMPLIANCE 7y local/landing
mc mb local/warehouse                                # Iceberg tables: NO object lock (see 5.3)

mc cp ./NAVAll.txt local/landing/source=amfi-nav/received=2026-10-31/sha256=9f2c…/original.txt
mc rm local/landing/source=amfi-nav/…/original.txt   # adds a delete marker; the version is retained
mc retention info local/landing/source=amfi-nav/…/original.txt

Writing from Python with boto3:

import boto3
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

s3 = boto3.client("s3", endpoint_url="http://localhost:9000",
                  aws_access_key_id="admin", aws_secret_access_key="password123")

s3.put_object(
    Bucket="landing", Key=key, Body=data,
    ChecksumSHA256=base64_sha256,                        # server verifies the bytes it stored
    ObjectLockMode="COMPLIANCE",
    ObjectLockRetainUntilDate=datetime.now(timezone.utc) + timedelta(days=7 * 365),
)

5.3 Where not to put WORM

Iceberg tables rewrite and delete files during maintenance (compaction, snapshot expiry, orphan cleanup). Put Object Lock on the landing bucket only. The table warehouse bucket gets versioning and normal access controls, and its history is protected by Iceberg snapshots and tags instead.

6. The unified collector

All sources share one framework; only the adapter differs.

---
title: Collector flow into immutable landing
---
flowchart TD
    REG["Source and rights register"] --> SCH["Scheduler"]
    SCH --> AD{"Adapter"}
    AD --> HTTP["HTTP / API"]
    AD --> SFTP["SFTP"]
    AD --> CDC["Database CDC<br/>(Debezium)"]
    AD --> STR["Stream<br/>(Kafka / Redpanda)"]
    HTTP --> HASH["Compute SHA-256"]
    SFTP --> HASH
    CDC --> HASH
    STR --> HASH
    HASH --> SEEN{"Hash seen before?"}
    SEEN -->|yes| SKIP["Record duplicate delivery"]
    SEEN -->|no| LAND["Write to locked landing bucket"]
    LAND --> MAN["Write manifest row"]
    MAN --> EVT["Emit 'file landed' event"]

from typing import Protocol, Iterator

class Fetched(Protocol):
    original_filename: str
    content_type: str
    data: bytes

class SourceAdapter(Protocol):
    source_id: str
    def fetch(self) -> Iterator[Fetched]: ...

def collect(adapter: SourceAdapter, register, store, manifests):
    rights = register.get(adapter.source_id)
    if not rights.may_store():
        raise PermissionError(f"No storage rights for {adapter.source_id}")
    for item in adapter.fetch():
        digest = hashlib.sha256(item.data).hexdigest()
        if manifests.exists(digest):
            manifests.record_duplicate(digest, adapter.source_id)
            continue
        key = store.put_locked(adapter.source_id, digest, item)
        manifests.insert(digest=digest, key=key, source_id=adapter.source_id,
                         licence_id=rights.licence_id, filename=item.original_filename)

6.1 Change data capture and streams

  • CDC with Debezium reads the database's change log (PostgreSQL WAL, SQL Server CDC tables, MySQL binlog) and emits one event per insert/update/delete to Kafka. You get every change, not periodic snapshots.
  • Kafka / Redpanda hold those events durably. A landing consumer writes them in batches (e.g. one Parquet or JSON-lines file per partition per 5 minutes), hashes each batch and lands it like any file.

More on CDC and streaming: Data processing types, Streaming pipelines.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why is the original filename a poor key for a landed file?
  2. What does a DELETE do to an object under Compliance-mode retention?
  3. Why does the Iceberg warehouse bucket not use Object Lock?
  4. A provider re-sends yesterday's file with one changed row. What happens at file level and at record level?
  5. Which fields of the manifest let you prove, a year later, where a number came from?

8. Review checklist

  • Landing stores original bytes, keyed by SHA-256.
  • Landing bucket created with Object Lock; default retention set.
  • Every file has a manifest row with source, licence and collector version.
  • The collector checks the rights register before fetching.
  • Duplicate deliveries are recorded, not re-processed.
